title: Managing Secrets in Pipelines
intro: Pipelines need credentials to deploy — which makes them one of the most attractive targets for attackers. These habits keep secrets out of code, logs, and git history.

steps.prompt: Store a deploy token as a repository secret, reading its value from a local file instead of typing it on the command line.
steps.fake_output: ✓ Set Actions secret DEPLOY_TOKEN for acme/shop
steps.explanation: The value is encrypted and only exposed to workflows at runtime, as ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}.
steps.why: 'gh secret set DEPLOY_TOKEN --body "abc123"' works, but leaves the secret in your shell history. Reading from a file (or an interactive prompt) avoids that.

steps.prompt: Store a production-only database password scoped to the 'production' environment.
expected_commands: gh secret set DB_PASSWORD --env production < db_pass.txt
gh secret set DB_PASSWORD -e production < db_pass.txt
steps.fake_output: ✓ Set Actions secret DB_PASSWORD for acme/shop (production)
steps.explanation: Environment secrets are only available to jobs that declare 'environment: production'.
steps.why: Environments can require manual approval and restrict which branches may deploy to them. That means a PR from a random branch can't read production secrets — repo-level secrets are much broader.

steps.prompt: List the repository's secrets to audit what exists.
steps.fake_output:
NAME          UPDATED
DEPLOY_TOKEN  about 1 minute ago
NPM_TOKEN     about 2 years ago
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY  about 3 years ago
steps.explanation: Names and update dates only — values can never be read back.
steps.why: A 3-year-old static AWS key is a red flag. Modern pipelines use OIDC (workflow requests short-lived cloud credentials by proving its identity), which removes long-lived cloud keys from CI entirely.

steps.prompt: Locally, load variables from a .env file into your current shell to reproduce what the pipeline sees.
steps.explanation: Every KEY=value line in .env is now an environment variable in this shell.
steps.why: The 'export $(cat .env | xargs)' trick breaks on values with spaces or quotes; 'set -a; source .env; set +a' is more robust. Either way, .env must be in .gitignore.

steps.prompt: Before committing, scan the repo for accidentally committed secrets.
steps.fake_output:
Finding:     AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG...
File:        scripts/old-deploy.sh
Commit:      8c9d0e1

1 leaks found
steps.explanation: A real AWS key in an old script, still in git history.
steps.why: Scanners like gitleaks/trufflehog belong in a pre-commit hook and in CI. Once a secret is pushed, deleting it isn't enough — history keeps it, so it must be rotated (see cicd-incident-004).
